description: Interests: combustion physics, spacecraft fire safety, AI for science. Skills: mechanical design, thermo/physics modeling, optimization  Why join: we'll build an AI-powered dashboard that ranks and interprets NASA PSI combustion data for Moon/Mars fire safety, with a working prototype, not just slides. Looking for: web dev (React/Python), data science/LLMs (RAG), combustion/CFD background, data visualization, UX, pitch.
summary:
AstroSense is a web-based simulation engine for fire safety in microgravity. It turns NASA’s open fire research records (PSI, including BASS, SAFFIRE, SAME and FLEX) into a clear traffic-light decision. Users choose a material, change parameters such as pressure, oxygen, temperature and aerosols, and run a test. The engine compares each parameter against research-based limits, using complex mathematical models that include Navier-Stokes-based CFD, and returns a safety score out of 100 with an explanation of what caused the risk. Flamy, a multi-agent AI assistant powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, answers questions using the challenge data.

The project addresses the challenge by making NASA’s fire research easy to explore, understand and apply, without costly or risky physical tests. It matters because fire in a spacecraft is one of the most dangerous events for a crew, and flames behave very differently in microgravity. Our next step is to replace manual input with automatic sensors.

details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AstroSense is a simulation engine for fire safety in microgravity. It turns NASA research records (the PSI records) into a clear traffic-light decision. Fire behaves differently in space: without natural convection, flames form spheres and can burn in ways that are hard to predict, and a closed cabin leaves little margin for error. Testing this on real hardware is costly and risky, so AstroSense lets anyone explore it virtually.

The platform is divided into four modules: Fire Safety, Fire Extinguisher, Predictive Modeling of Flammability and Fire Scenarios, and Flame Group. Each module is split into sections by research study (for example BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SAME and FLEX, the Flame Extinguishment Experiment with 274 tests using methanol and heptane), and each study is shown with its data and charts.

The simulation

The simulation is the core of AstroSense. It combines complex mathematical models from NASA research, including the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases move and are the foundation of the thermo-convective CFD model. This lets the engine capture how heat, gases and flames behave when gravity is almost absent.

The analysis adapts to three things:

The material or fuel. The user selects the sample to analyze, such as methanol, heptane or n-dodecane for liquid fuels, or solids such as PMMA, SIBAL fabric, Nomex, Ultem, and candles and wax. Each material has its own limits taken from the research. For example, the limiting oxygen index (LOI) of the material, the critical oxygen level for methanol, its optimal pressure range, and the cold-flame window of n-dodecane.

The parameters. The user changes variables such as cabin pressure, oxygen level, flame temperature, aerosol concentration, smoke density, flame spread rate, radiative heat flux, cooling rate, droplet diameter and velocity gradient. The result updates according to these values.

The test or scenario. The user chooses the study or module to run (Fire Safety, Flame Group, flame dissipation or predictive modeling) and can load presets: Nominal, Cold Flame and Critical.

Inside the engine, each parameter is compared against its limit from the research. If it exceeds the limit, it subtracts points from a safety score out of 100. For example, a critical oxygen level subtracts 45 points, out-of-range pressure subtracts 18, high aerosols subtract 15, and the cold-flame window subtracts 12. The result is a traffic-light decision with a safety score and a technical log that explains which parameters caused the risk.

The Predictive Modeling module uses three mathematical models from NASA research:

PSI-60 SPICE: soot volume fraction, pyrometric temperature, optical density and frame rate.

PSI-62 FGM: flame spread rate, ignition probability, pyrolysis heat flux and solid density.

PSI-117 thermo-convective CFD (based on Navier-Stokes): convective perturbation, oscillation amplitude, pressure and mesh nodes.

It shows a soot and thermal heat map with three states: Prediction Stable, Perturbation Detected and Instability / Divergence.

Worked example with n-dodecane: a cold-flame scenario (1.0 atm, 21% O₂, 700 K, 420 particles/cm³) scores 84/100 with moderate risk. A critical scenario (0.10 atm, 11.5% O₂, 480 K, 780 particles/cm³) scores 18/100 with imminent extinction and high risk.

Today the parameters are entered manually. Our plan is to replace manual entry with sensors that measure oxygen, pressure, temperature, smoke and heat flux automatically and feed the models in real time, so the traffic-light decision updates by itself.

The AI layer

An AI layer supports users. Four chatbots were built with all the information from the challenge repositories. Flamy, our research assistant, coordinates them and has two modes: a Web mode that searches the internet, and a Database mode that uses the multi-agent system based on the repository data.

What benefits does it have?

It makes complex microgravity combustion research easy to explore and understand without special equipment or risk. Every study is charted and explained. Every simulation gives a clear, explainable decision rather than just numbers, showing which parameter caused the risk, and it adapts to the material and the test. Users can also ask Flamy questions in plain language, in Spanish or English.

What is the intended impact?

To make NASA’s open fire research easier for students, researchers and the public to use, and to show why fire safety is a unique challenge in space exploration. The traffic-light approach turns research data into an easy-to-read safety decision. It is an educational and research demo, not an operational emergency system. Our next step is to connect real sensors so the analysis runs automatically, which could eventually support early fire detection in spacecraft cabins.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, plus React / Next.js, deployed on Vercel. All modules were integrated into a single web page.

AI-assisted development: we built the platform with Claude (Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot as coding assistants. Our team defined what to build, provided the scientific content, parameters and data, and then ran the generated code (for example, executing scripts in PowerShell to create the project files), tested the results, and iterated with the AI until everything worked as intended. This workflow let a multidisciplinary team of engineers, with only one member with programming experience, build a complete web application.

AI in the product: NVIDIA API. The four data chatbots run on Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Flamy, the coordinating assistant, runs on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning.

Data: NASA challenge repository data (PSI records, including the FLEX dataset) organized into tables for the chatbots, plus our own simulation tables and parameter limits built from scientific papers.

Scientific models: mathematical models from the research (SPICE, FGM and thermo-convective CFD based on the Navier-Stokes equations).

Hardware: none required today. All sensor readings are simulated. Sensors are planned for the next phase.

How is your project creative?

It converts research records into a decision-making tool: a safety score and a traffic-light result instead of raw data. It combines chemistry, mechanical engineering and AI in one interface. Complex mathematical models, including Navier-Stokes, run behind a simple interface that anyone can use by changing the material, the parameters and the test. It uses a multi-agent design in which specialized chatbots are coordinated by Flamy, a friendly assistant with online and database modes. It also visualizes how microgravity changes fire, using a soot and thermal heat map and preset scenarios (Nominal, Cold Flame and Critical).

What factors did your team consider?

Multidisciplinary teamwork: six students from Instituto Tecnológico de Aguascalientes (TECNM) in ICT, mechanical engineering, chemical engineering and a master’s in AI.

Mayra Vanessa Capetillo González (ICT) integrated everything into a single web page and led the technical integration.

Emilio Yain Rubalcava Esquivel (Mechanical) built the four chatbots with the information from the challenge repositories.

Harold Jarek Bonilla López (Mechanical) built the AI that coordinates the chatbots, including its internet mode.

Hannia Espinoza Huerta (Chemical) developed the chemical side: the simulation based on the parameters and the mathematical model.

Juan Luis Pedroza Mota (Mechanical) helped with the presentation.

Fernando Chávez Valdivia (Master’s in AI) served as the team’s technical mentor, guiding us across every area of the project, from AI and data to simulation logic and overall direction.

Scientific grounding: limits and penalties come from the research and from scientific papers, and every study is charted.

Data grounding: the chatbots answer from the repository data to reduce made-up answers.

Responsible AI use: we used AI coding assistants openly as part of our workflow. The team decided what the platform should do, supplied the science (parameters, limits, penalties and models from NASA research and papers), and tested and verified that each part worked before integrating it. The chemical and mechanical engineers guided and checked the scientific results.

Transparency: the app states that it is a simulation for educational purposes and that chat messages are sent to an external service.

Accessibility: a clear interface and traffic-light results for people without technical backgrounds.

Scalability: the design allows adding more studies, fuels and materials, and replacing manual input with automatic sensors.
